content.text:
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We begin with very important properties of positive integers, namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b in such a way that it leaves a remainder r that is smaller than b. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way - this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics.

We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as √2, √3 and √5. Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal expansion of a rational number, say p/q (q ≠ 0), is terminating and when it is non-terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator q of p/q. You will see that the prime factorisation of q will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of p/q.

So let us begin our exploration.

In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, 253 = 11 × 23, and so on. Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.

Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish, we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many). Let us list a few :
7 × 11 × 23 = 1771
3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 5313
2 × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 10626
2³ × 3 × 7³ = 8232
2² × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 21252
and so on.

Now, let us suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes. What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite number of integers, or infinitely many? Infact, there are infinitely many primes. So, if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite collection of numbers, all the primes and all possible products of primes. The question is - can we produce all the composite numbers this way? What do you think? Do you think that there may be a composite number which is not the product of powers of primes? Before we answer this, let us factorise positive integers, that is, do the opposite of what we have done so far.

content.text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any composite number it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a 'unique' way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as long as we are not particular about the order in which the primes occur. So, for example, we regard 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 as the same as 3 × 5 × 7 × 2, or any other possible order in which these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:

The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order of its factors.

In general, given a composite number x, we factorise it as x = p₁p₂ ... pₙ, where p₁, p₂,..., pₙ are primes and written in ascending order, i.e., p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ . . . ≤ pₙ. If we combine the same primes, we will get powers of primes. For example, 32760 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 13 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13

Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number is factorised, is unique.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples.

Q. Check that 3803 and 3607 are primes, and that 3² × 3803 × 3607 really is 123456789.
A. To test a number, divide it by every prime up to its square root: the primes up to 61 for 3803, and up to 59 for 3607. None divides exactly, so both are prime. Then 9 × 3803 × 3607 = 123456789.

You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it! This method is also called the prime factorisation method. Let us recall this method through an example.

Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.

We have : 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2 × 2 × 5 = 2² × 5¹.

Note that HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.

media.title: What Makes a Number Irrational
media.description: A 150-second introduction video. Scene 1 shows the definition card 'Irrational: cannot be written p/q, integers, q ≠ 0'. Scene 2 tests √9 - √9 = 3 = 3/1 with a green tick; it is rational. Scene 3 tests √2 - a bar labelled 'try all p/q' scrolls through 1/1, 3/2, 7/5, 99/70, … ; the decimals get closer to 1.41421356… but a decimal panel flags 'non-terminating, non-repeating - no p/q matches'. Scene 4 declares the list √2, √3, √15, π, √2/√3, 0.10110111011110… irrational. Text-only annotations, blue and red palette.
media.teaching_notes: Play this explainer at the START of Section 1.3, before students look at Theorem 1.2 in Topic T11. Pause at 55s and ask 'Before we check √15 - is it rational or irrational, and why?' - this is the attempt-before-reveal moment; accept any reasoning about the p/q test, then resume. Pause at 115s and ask 'Does scrolling through fractions actually prove √2 is irrational?' - lead students to the answer that it only suggests irrationality; the formal proof needs Theorem 1.2. After the video, ask 'How is √9 different from √2 despite both being written with a radical?' to surface the ERROR ALERT.

content.text:
In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties. You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. Here, we will prove that √2, √3, √5 and, in general, √p is irrational, where p is a prime. One of the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Recall, a number 's' is called irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Some examples of irrational numbers, with which you are already familiar, are :
√2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3, 0.10110111011110 …, etc.

concepts.concept_name: If a prime divides a², it divides a: try it first

content.text:
Let the prime factorisation of a be as follows :
a = p₁p₂ . . . pₙ, where p₁, p₂, . . ., pₙ are primes, not necessarily distinct.

Therefore, a² = (p₁p₂ . . . pₙ)(p₁p₂ . . . pₙ) = p₁²p₂² . . . pₙ².

Now, we are given that p divides a². Therefore, from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, it follows that p is one of the prime factors of a². However, using the uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, we realise that the only prime factors of a² are p₁, p₂, . . ., pₙ. So p is one of p₁, p₂, . . ., pₙ.

Now, since a = p₁p₂ . . . pₙ, p divides a.

content.text:
Let us assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational.

So, we can find integers r and s (≠ 0) such that √2 = r/s.

Suppose r and s have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common factor to get √2 = a/b, where a and b are coprime.

So, b√2 = a.

Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get 2b² = a². Therefore, 2 divides a².

Now, by the theorem that if a prime divides a² then it divides a, it follows that 2 divides a.

So, we can write a = 2c for some integer c.

Substituting for a, we get 2b² = 4c², that is, b² = 2c².

This means that 2 divides b², and so 2 divides b (again using that theorem with p = 2).

Therefore, a and b have at least 2 as a common factor.

But this contradicts the fact that a and b have no common factors other than 1.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that √2 is rational.

So, we conclude that √2 is irrational.

content.text: Prove that √3 is irrational.
content.question: Prove that √3 is irrational.
content.publication_text: Prove that √3 is irrational.

content.text:
Let us assume, to the contrary, that √3 is rational.

That is, we can find integers a and b (≠ 0) such that √3 = a/b.

Suppose a and b have a common factor other than 1, then we can divide by the common factor, and assume that a and b are coprime.

So, b√3 = a.

Squaring on both sides, and rearranging, we get 3b² = a².

Therefore, a² is divisible by 3, and by the theorem that if a prime divides a² then it divides a, it follows that a is also divisible by 3.

So, we can write a = 3c for some integer c.

Substituting for a, we get 3b² = 9c², that is, b² = 3c².

This means that b² is divisible by 3, and so b is also divisible by 3 (using that theorem with p = 3).

Therefore, a and b have at least 3 as a common factor.

But this contradicts the fact that a and b are coprime.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that √3 is rational.

So, we conclude that √3 is irrational.

That is, we can find coprime a and b (b ≠ 0) such that 5 - √3 = a/b.

Therefore, 5 - a/b = √3.

Rearranging this equation, we get √3 = 5 - a/b = (5b - a)/b.

Since a and b are integers, we get 5 - a/b is rational, and so √3 is rational.

But this contradicts the fact that √3 is irrational.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that 5 - √3 is rational.

So, we conclude that 5 - √3 is irrational.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In Class IX, you met irrational numbers for the first time and placed a few of them on the real number line. This chapter takes that story further by returning to the positive integers with a simple question. What are the building blocks of every natural number, and what can those blocks tell us about numbers that are not whole?

RECALL: You already know that a prime number has exactly two factors, namely 1 and itself, while a composite number has more than two factors.

CORE: Section 1.2 focuses on two very important properties of positive integers. The first is Euclid's division algorithm. Stated simply, it says that any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b so that it leaves a remainder r smaller than b. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although the result is straightforward to state, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers, and we will use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The second property is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. This theorem has to do with the multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way, and that one sentence is essentially the whole theorem. Easy to state, yet it has very deep applications. We will use it for two main purposes in this chapter. First, we will prove the irrationality of numbers such as √2, √3 and √5, numbers you only accepted as irrational in Class IX. Second, we will apply it to determine exactly when the decimal expansion of a rational number p/q (q ≠ 0) terminates and when it is non-terminating repeating. The prime factorisation of the denominator q will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of p/q.

MULTIPLYING PRIMES TO BUILD NUMBERS: In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, and 253 = 11 × 23, and so on. Now let us look at natural numbers from the other direction. Can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers together in some combination? That question is the door into this chapter.

ERROR ALERT: Many students initially think primes are rare curiosities used only for factor-tree exercises. In reality, primes are the atoms of the positive integers: every composite number is assembled from them.

CHECK: In one sentence, how would you explain to a Class IX student why Euclid's division algorithm is really just the long-division procedure they already use?
carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
1.1 Introduction

In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b in such a way that it leaves a remainder r that is smaller than b. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way - this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics. We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as √2, √3 and √5. Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal expansion of a rational number, say p/q (q ≠ 0), is terminating and when it is non-terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator q of p/q. You will see that the prime factorisation of q will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of p/q.

So let us begin our exploration.

1.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, 253 = 11 × 23, and so on. Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.
concept_bullets: Euclid's division algorithm is just the usual long-division fact - for example, dividing 17 by 5 gives quotient 3 and remainder 2, with 2 < 5.
Every composite number is built from primes by multiplication - for example, 253 = 11 × 23 and 4 = 2 × 2, combining primes from a small pantry.
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic is later used to prove that numbers such as √2, √3 and √5 are irrational.
The prime factorisation of the denominator q tells us whether the decimal expansion of p/q terminates or is non-terminating repeating.

Euclid's division algorithm is the familiar long-division fact that any positive integer a, when divided by a positive integer b, leaves a remainder r smaller than b; it is the chapter's main tool for computing HCFs. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number factorises into primes uniquely, and it is used later in the chapter both to compute HCF and LCM and to prove that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational. For example, 253 = 11 × 23 and 4 = 2 × 2 show the "build-up" direction, while any number can also be decomposed downward into primes. Students use this orientation whenever they meet a problem about divisibility, factorisation, or irrationality in the rest of the chapter.
important_points: We begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b in such a way that it leaves a remainder r that is smaller than b.
every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way - this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

recall_questions.answer: In the build-up direction, we start with primes and multiply them in different combinations to produce natural numbers (e.g., 2 x 2 = 4, 11 x 23 = 253). In the factor-tree direction, we start with a composite number and keep splitting it until only primes remain. Both directions show that every natural number is built from primes, so primes are the atoms of the positive integers.

carried_over_topics.summary: Theorem 1.1, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, states that every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes, and that this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the prime factors. The method is the factor tree: pick any prime that divides the number cleanly, split, and repeat on each composite branch until only primes remain. For example, the factor tree for 32760 - 32760 → 2 × 16380 → 2 × 8190 → 2 × 4095 → 3 × 1365 → 3 × 455 → 5 × 91 → 7 × 13 - gives 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13 in prime-power form. Writing primes in ascending order makes this representation unique, which is the reason the theorem supports every later HCF, LCM and irrationality argument in the chapter.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Take any small collection of primes and multiply them in different combinations. Can you reach every composite number you can think of, or will some remain out of reach? This topic answers that question decisively.

RECALL: From the previous topic, we want to look at natural numbers from the build-up direction: starting with primes and multiplying them to produce larger numbers.

CORE - Building numbers from primes: Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish, we can produce a large collection of positive integers. In fact, we can produce infinitely many. Let us list a few:

7 × 11 × 23 = 1771
3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 5313
2 × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 10626
2³ × 3 × 7³ = 8232
2² × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 21252

and so on.

Now suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes. What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite number of integers, or infinitely many? In fact, there are infinitely many primes. So, if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite collection of numbers: all the primes and all possible products of primes. The natural question is - can we produce all the composite numbers this way? Do you think there may be a composite number which is not the product of powers of primes?

FACTORISING IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: Before answering, let us factorise positive integers; that is, do the opposite of what we have done so far. We will use the factor tree with which you are familiar. Consider the large number 32760 and factorise it step by step:

32760 → 2 × 16380 → 2 × 8190 → 2 × 4095 → 3 × 1365 → 3 × 455 → 5 × 91 → 7 × 13

So we have factorised 32760 as 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 13, i.e., 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13 as a product of powers of primes.

WHY THIS STEP? We kept dividing by the smallest prime that divides cleanly. Why? Because it guarantees we end only when every remaining factor is prime, so the tree terminates and gives us an honest prime factorisation.

Let us try another number, say 123456789. This can be written as 3² × 3803 × 3607. Of course, you have to check that 3803 and 3607 are primes. (Try it out for several other natural numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and it is called the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic because of its basic, crucial importance to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic): Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

HISTORICAL NOTE: An equivalent version of Theorem 1.1 was probably first recorded as Proposition 14 of Book IX in Euclid's Elements, before it came to be known as the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. However, the first correct proof was given by Carl Friedrich Gauss in his Disquisitiones Arithmeticae. Carl Friedrich Gauss is often referred to as the 'Prince of Mathematicians' and is considered one of the three greatest mathematicians of all time, along with Archimedes and Newton. He has made fundamental contributions to both mathematics and science.

UNPACKING THE WORD "UNIQUE": The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any composite number, it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a unique way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as long as we are not particular about the order in which the primes are written. So, for example, we regard 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 as the same as 3 × 5 × 7 × 2, or any other possible order in which these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:

The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order of its factors.

GENERAL FORM: Given a composite number x, we factorise it as x = p₁p₂…pₙ, where p₁, p₂, …, pₙ are primes written in ascending order, i.e., p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ … ≤ pₙ. If we combine the same primes, we get powers of primes. For example, 32760 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 13 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13.

WHY THIS STEP? We agreed to write the primes in ascending order. Why? Because once the order is fixed, the factorisation is determined completely; there is no room for two different-looking prime lists to describe the same number.

Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number is factorised is unique.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is to think that "unique" forbids writing 2 × 3 × 5 in any other sequence. Uniqueness here means uniqueness of the multiset of primes, not the order of the symbols on the page.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples in the next few topics.

CHECK: The number 32760 has been written as 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13. If a classmate wrote 13 × 7 × 5 × 3² × 2³ instead, would you accept it as the same prime factorisation? Justify using Theorem 1.1.

carried_over_topics.summary: This worked example uses Theorem 1.1's uniqueness clause to rule out an entire family of endings. The question is whether 4ⁿ - for any natural number n - can ever end in the digit 0. The method: ending in 0 means divisible by 10, hence divisible by 5; so 5 must appear in the prime factorisation. The key insight: 4ⁿ = (2)²ⁿ, so 2 is the only prime ever appearing in the factorisation of 4ⁿ, and uniqueness in Theorem 1.1 forbids any other prime from sneaking in. Hence there is no natural number n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero. This technique transfers to any number of the form aⁿ where a's prime factorisation is missing a prime the question demands.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Can a power of 4 ever end in 0? Theorem 1.1 answers decisively.

WORKED EXAMPLE - Example 1: Consider the numbers 4ⁿ, where n is a natural number. Check whether there is any value of n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

Solution: If the number 4ⁿ, for any n, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be divisible by 5. That is, the prime factorisation of 4ⁿ would contain the prime 5. This is not possible because 4ⁿ = (2)²ⁿ; so the only prime in the factorisation of 4ⁿ is 2. So, the uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no other primes in the factorisation of 4ⁿ. So, there is no natural number n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

WHY THIS STEP? "Ends in 0" means divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so 5 must appear in the factorisation.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is that for large n, 4ⁿ eventually picks up a 5. Multiplication cannot create new primes; 5 never enters a product of copies of 4.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1: If 4^n ended with the digit 0, it would be divisible by 10 = 2 x 5, so 5 would appear in the prime factorisation of 4^n. Step 2: But 4^n = (2^2)^n = 2^(2n), so the only prime in the factorisation of 4^n is 2. Step 3: By the uniqueness part of Theorem 1.1, no other prime can appear in the factorisation of 4^n, so 5 is not a factor of 4^n. Conclusion: there is no natural number n for which 4^n ends with the digit zero.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, show whether there is any natural number n for which 4^n ends with the digit zero.

recall_questions.answer: A positive integer ends with the digit 0 exactly when it is divisible by 10. Since 10 = 2 x 5, being divisible by 10 is the same as being divisible by both 2 and 5. So checking whether 4^n ends in 0 reduces to checking whether its prime factorisation contains both 2 and 5.
recall_questions.prompt: Why does the phrase 'ends with the digit zero' translate to 'divisible by both 2 and 5' in this argument?

recall_questions.answer: 25^n = (5^2)^n = 5^(2n), so the only prime in the factorisation of 25^n is 5. For 25^n to end in 0, it would need 2 as a prime factor (since 10 = 2 x 5). By the uniqueness clause of Theorem 1.1, no prime other than 5 appears in 25^n, so 2 is not a factor. Therefore, 25^n can never end with the digit zero.

Starting together at the gate, when will they next be at the gate at the same moment? The meeting time must be a multiple of both 4 and 6, so we need the smallest common multiple - the LCM.

CORE - Rule for LCM by prime factorisation:

LCM(6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor, involved in the numbers.
